reasoning: A calls this definitional recall, but the stem never states the definition — it describes a governance arrangement (no reporting line to the reviewed unit, results routed to the audit committee) and asks what property that structure establishes. Classifying a described case into a concept is an Understand process in Anderson and Krathwohl, not Remember; Remember covers retrieval from a memorised set. Independence, attestation, non-repudiation, and due diligence are not one memorised taxonomy the candidate can index into — they are scattered terms, so the discrimination has to run through the described case. A's own file confirms this: it tags 2lk8XPsECfnMbfqjOipV (chain of custody derived from a described forensic procedure, identical shape) as Understand with the reason that the candidate must interpret a described practice rather than recall a definition. A is internally inconsistent across the pair and Understand is the correct side of it.

A argues the task is naming the attack, not reasoning about it. But the keyed answer is a compound (typosquatting used as the delivery mechanism for phishing), and each distractor is ruled out only by interpreting a stated fact: the bank's real domain is untouched, so nothing was hijacked; no resolver is involved, so it is not cache poisoning; nothing is intercepted, so it is not on-path. Distinguishing 'registered a lookalike the attacker controls' from 'took over the real domain' is an interpretive step, not a lookup. A tags IzQnAi2oN7wdcd1fggoR (supply chain compromise inferred from a described chain, then separated from similar-sounding categories) as Understand for exactly this reasoning — the same shape gets the same level.

I was wrong. I reached for Analyze because the item asks the candidate to distinguish two things, and I mapped 'differentiating' onto that. That is a misreading of the taxonomy: in Anderson and Krathwohl, comparing — detecting correspondences and differences between two ideas — is an Understand process, while Analyze's differentiating means separating relevant from irrelevant parts within presented material. Here there is no material to decompose; both assessment types are named in the stem and the candidate explains what each one verifies. The budget conflict is framing, not cognitive load.

I was wrong. That is assessment procedure applied to a situation.

I was wrong. I treated the minimal-suppression carve-out as a settled rule to be applied, which underrates the item. Two obligations genuinely conflict here — the erasure right against the need to keep honouring a do-not-contact instruction — and every distractor is a position practitioners actually argue: legitimate interest to refuse, delete everything and let the customer re-opt-out, anonymise and retain for analytics. No single procedure outputs the answer; the candidate has to reason about proportionality and decide how far erasure extends and on what legal basis the remainder survives. Weighing competing obligations and justifying the boundary is Evaluate.

I was wrong. I equated 'critique a proposed design' with Evaluate, but Evaluate requires judging against criteria or weighing alternatives, and neither happens here. There is one design, one flaw, and the task is to explain the causal chain: the key beside the ciphertext means a single host compromise yields plaintext, so the control buys nothing. Explaining cause and effect is an Understand process. A's further point is decisive — the three distractors are simply false statements about what PCI DSS requires, so eliminating them draws on factual knowledge rather than judgement.

This stem states the discriminator outright — mandatory intent ('must use multifactor authentication') with no products or configuration steps — which is the textbook separation of policy from standard, procedure, and guideline.
